https://hungarytoday.hu/colombian-commun.text: Colombian Community Fights to Save Its Embassy in Budapest Diplomatic relations between Colombia and Hungary are facing a critical test. Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella, who will take office on August 7, has announced far-reaching austerity and restructuring measures in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs that will also have a direct impact on Central Europe. The Colombian Embassy in Budapest is set to close after eight years of continuous presence. Civil society is now mobilizing in opposition to this move. A total of 14 countries worldwide—including three on the European continent—are affected by the cuts imposed by the South American oil power, which has a population of 50 million. According to the plans, Colombia will withdraw completely from Hungary, as well as from Romania and the Czech Republic. The newly elected president provided a broad range of justifications for this far-reaching change, which vary depending on the region. While he offered ideological grounds for the withdrawal from Latin America—emphasizing that the Colombian government does not maintain diplomatic relations with “tyrannies” such as Cuba and Nicaragua—in Europe, purely fiscal arguments take center stage. Abelardo de la Espriella justified the closure of the embassy in Budapest with the need for greater frugality in the use of public funds. “We cannot maintain such a costly structure that does not yield tangible results for the country,” the president stated on his social media page. Colombia needs a diplomatic approach that is modern and efficient and serves national interests, rather than “political favoritism and bureaucracy.” Abelardo de la Espriella. Photo: Wikipedia The measures are part of an “optimization process.” However, this does not constitute a complete break in diplomatic relations with the affected countries. The protection of Colombian citizens will be guaranteed in the future through a system of co-accreditation by other embassies in the region, the politician added. In Budapest, the news has caused considerable consternation. As Világgazdaság reports, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, led by Anita Orbán, was completely taken by surprise by the plans. The Hungarian ministry confirmed to the news portal that it had received no prior indication from Bogotá and had only learned of the move through the press. According to the news portal, the Hungarian TISZA government has no immediate plans to close its own embassy in Bogotá in retaliation. Nevertheless, bilateral relations have suffered a serious blow. Hungary established official diplomatic relations with Colombia in 1973. After the Hungarian mission was reopened in 2017 by Péter Szijjártó, then foreign minister from FIDESZ, the Colombian embassy in Budapest followed suit in 2018—an era that is now coming to an abrupt end. An exact date for the closure has not yet been officially set. Protests are now mounting against the plans. The Colombian community in Hungary and Central Europe/the Balkans announced in a statement that it has launched a citizen-led initiative, which will be officially presented on August 6. In a petition that has already been signed by more than 300 verified citizens of the region, President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella is urged to reconsider the decision. The signatories emphasize that the embassy and its attached consular section in Budapest provide indispensable services to residents, students, researchers, and families. The official consular district extends far beyond Hungary and also includes Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, North Macedonia, and Montenegro. Although only about 250 Colombians are officially registered in Hungary, the mission serves an estimated 600 to 1,200 Colombian nationals throughout Central Europe and the Western Balkans. Particular emphasis is placed on the embassy’s role for academics, for example through the Stipendium Hungaricum program, one of the most important educational partnerships between the two countries. In addition to everyday, essential services such as passport renewals, notarial matters, and document legalizations, the mission played a key role in providing emergency assistance, especially during the COVID-19 pandemic. Based on the statement, closing the mission in Budapest would force citizens to travel to distant embassies in other European countries for simple administrative procedures which would result in significant financial, logistical, and administrative burdens for those affected. The initiative, which continues to gather online support and physical signature lists, calls on the Colombian government to explore alternative cost-saving measures in order to protect the partnerships in culture and education that have been built up over more than five decades. The embassy in Budapest must not be abandoned, as it serves as an indispensable strategic bridge between Colombia and Central Europe. Russia-Ukraine War Poland Summons Russian Ambassador Over Cruise Missile Incursion A missile, determined by Polish authorities to have been manufactured near Moscow, landed near the city of Lublin on July 30. Save Mark Us Preferred on Google Print Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk in London on May 27, 2026. Jack Taylor/Reuters Guy Birchall 8/1/2026 | Updated: 8/2/2026 0:00 X 1 Poland summoned the Russian ambassador on July 31 over the incursion of a cruise missile that crashed near the Polish city of Lublin the day before . Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said, “Today, the Polish Foreign Ministry summoned the Russian ambassador in connection with the missile that hit Polish territory yesterday,” in a post on X. The Polish Ministry of Foreign Affairs confirmed in a post on X after the meeting that Moscow’s ambassador had been served with a protest note by Robert Kupiecki, who serves as the ministry’s undersecretary of state and as national security adviser to Tusk. The summoning of the ambassador came after Poland confirmed, following an investigation on July 30, that the missile was Russian. Polish Deputy Minister of National Defense Cezary Tomczyk told Polish radio station RMF24, in an interview on July 30, that the ministry “can confirm with full responsibility that it was a Russian Kh-101 missile. ... i.e. a cruise missile capable of carrying even nuclear warheads, which exploded on impact with the ground.” He noted that the missile that struck Polish territory was part of a 70-missile-strong barrage that Moscow’s forces launched against Ukraine, 20 of which were “flying towards Poland.” Related Stories Cruise Missile Hits Poland Amid Russian Strikes on Ukraine Finland Closes Southern Airspace, Waters Over Stray Drone Risk Tomczyk said that the bulk of these missiles were “shot down by Ukraine over Ukraine,” but that the pilot tracking the missile that eventually hit the country failed to neutralize it and then “turned back 20 seconds before the border” because of the risk of being shot down by a Polish F-16. Asked if the strike was intentionally launched at Poland, Tomczyk said the government currently did not know. “In the case of the drones shot down by the Polish Army on Sept. 10 of last year, I can say with certainty that it was no accident,” he said, calling it a provocation and a test of the NATO alliance. The crater left by the impact was about 30 feet wide, Polish Interior Ministry spokesperson Karolina Gałecka said in a July 30 post on X, noting that it was found a little more than a mile away from some buildings. Polish Deputy Prime Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz shed further light on the missile’s origin in a July 31 post on X. He said that the Military Gendarmerie had confirmed that it was “manufactured in the second quarter of this year at a factory near Moscow.” “This means that Russia is using missiles produced on an ongoing basis to attack Ukraine,” he said, noting that the information confirms reports that Russian military stockpiles have been depleted. The incident provoked widespread condemnation on July 30, with NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte calling it yet another reckless act by Russia and a dangerous consequence of its war against Ukraine, before reaffirming the alliance’s “unwavering” commitment to supporting Kyiv, in a post on X. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen also criticized Moscow over the incursion, calling it “another unacceptable violation of ... [European Union] airspace caused by Russia’s latest strikes on Ukraine” in a post on X. “To put an end to this, we are helping Ukraine win this war in every way we can,” she said. “And we are building a robust European security architecture on land, at sea and in the air.” U.S. Ambassador to Poland Tom Rose said that his embassy was “in constant contact” with the Polish government, U.S. Ambassador to NATO Matt Whitaker, and U.S. President Donald Trump over the incident, saying in a July 30 post on X, “Any breach of a NATO ally’s territory is a matter we take extremely seriously.” “We were lucky and grateful there were no casualties,” he said. “The United States stands firmly with Poland. We are coordinating closely with Polish authorities as the investigation proceeds and remain committed to defending Allied territory and upholding NATO’s collective security.” Despite the summoning of its ambassador by Poland, Moscow has not yet officially commented on the incident. However, the Russian Defense Ministry confirmed in a July 30 post on Telegram that it had “launched a massive strike using long-range air, land, and sea-based precision weapons, as well as attack drones, against military industrial facilities, telecommunications and logistics centers” across a range of cities in Ukraine. https://aa.com.tr/en/europe/polish-premi.text: Europe Polish premier rejects referendum on suspending participation in parts of Schengen area Proposal from former Premier Morawiecki's political camp would allow temporary suspension of free travel across land borders Jo Harper 20 August 2026 • Update : 20 August 2026 Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk on Thursday rejected a proposal from former Premier Mateusz Morawiecki’s political camp to hold a referendum on temporarily suspending Poland’s participation in parts of the Schengen free-travel area. The proposal emerged from a migration policy program presented by Morawiecki’s newly formed parliamentary group, Development Plus (Rozwoj Plus), which has been outlining policy positions ahead of parliamentary elections expected next year. Under the plan, Poland could consider temporarily suspending its participation in the land component of the Schengen system if tighter controls were deemed necessary for national security. Development Plus lawmaker Lukasz Schreiber said Poles should be asked to choose between greater freedom of travel and increased security. “If [people want] more security, perhaps we need to hold a referendum and even temporarily suspend our participation in the Schengen area, at least as regards land borders,” Schreiber said. The broader plan proposes creating a dedicated migration and assimilation ministry and a separate deportation service, introducing annual limits on labor migration and tightening border controls. It also calls for stronger assimilation requirements for foreigners and incentives for Poles living abroad to return home. The dispute is politically sensitive because Poland has itself temporarily restored checks on some internal Schengen borders at various points while simultaneously strengthening its external frontier with Belarus. Tusk’s government argues that protecting Poland’s external border is necessary precisely to preserve freedom of movement within Schengen. Poland’s current foreign policy strategy states that strengthened controls on the Belarusian frontier are intended to “safeguard the continued ability to exercise the free movement of people within the Schengen Area.” Migration has become an important political battleground for Morawiecki since his break with the Law and Justice (PiS) leadership and the recent formation of Development Plus. The new parliamentary group was created in late July following a prolonged internal conflict within PiS and initially brought together around 40 lawmakers. news_share news_share_description subscription_contact subscription LATEST NEWS All Hamilton hopeful Ferrari can win at Monza with engine upgrade Kenya's president orders India's Tata Chemicals to leave country Hull City condemns racist abuse targeting new signing Robinio Vaz Tel Aviv threatens Iran with strikes on energy facilities if it attacks Israel France records hottest summer since 1900 Beijing urges US to lift Iran-related sanctions on Chinese companies Swedish military intelligence chief warns of ‘high threat’ from Russian hybrid warfare See All Finland prepares to resume asylum seeker transfers to Italy UK asylum seekers warned against rape, harassment, ‘kissing sounds’ at people

https://www.cp24.com/news/entertainment/.text: TORONTO – A made-in-Canada production, filmed along the shores of Vancouver Island, is set to make a streaming splash this coming October. CTV’s parent company, Bell Media, is set to release a Crave original series titled “Yaga.” A supernatural thriller, the series title is taken from the pages of Slovak folklore, which feature an infamous witch. The centuries-old Slavic legend of “Baba Yaga” takes hold as a modern mystery thriller set in a small coastal community. The story follows a private investigator searching for a missing young heir to a powerful family, only to uncover a much darker web of secrets, hidden lives and ancient folklore. Carrie-Anne Moss, one of the show’s co-stars, says “Yaga” exposes the darker side of femininity. “It’s this part where you let go of being nice, where you let go of being a good girl, and you find yourself,” said Moss, who rose to worldwide prominence for her role as Trinity in “The Matrix.” The cast features numerous Canadians, including “Schitt’s Creek” star Noha Reid, “Letterkenny’s” Clark Backo, and Hudson Williams, who’s quickly becoming a household name following his leading role in “Heated Rivalry.” Sitting down with CTV News ahead of the show’s special screening at the Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF), Reid shared that filming the Canadian production, on Vancouver Island with a largely Canadian cast, is a point of pride. “When you get the opportunity to contribute to our cultural landscape, it feels really good to be involved in a production, particularly at this time, it feels like (the series) it’s Canadian in its bones,” said Reid. While walking to work, Moss shares that she would often think that “all the people (on set) are getting employed because of this job, right? From every department. That means a lot to me. People are paying their mortgages, putting their kids through school, that means a lot to me.” Based on the award-winning stage play by Canadian writer and showrunner Kat Sandler, the series brings the supernatural elements of the original story into a contemporary Canadian setting. Those familiar with Vancouver Island will note the familiar scenery. The show’s trailer features several notable locations, including Oak Bay’s historic Kiwanis Tea Room at Willows Beach, while the region’s coastline and forests help create the show’s eerie atmosphere. The eight episodes were shot in just 32 days. While the cast admit it was a lot of work to cover over such a short amount of time, the setting in and around Victoria had a “witchy vibe” that elevated the entire production. Williams wasn’t in Toronto for the sit-down interview with CTV News, but the cast shared that following “Heated Rivalry,” Williams is becoming a star in real-time. In “Yaga,” he plays two separate characters named Henry and Logan. “He came so prepared, everything was so well versed, he came in knowing exactly how he was going to differentiate these two characters,” Backo said. “It really did feel like two different people, which made our jobs so much easier, because the storyline (playing two characters) could have gotten confusing. But he plays a masterful job.” Audiences this week in Toronto will get a private screening at TIFF of the first two 30-minute episodes of the series. While Backo says she’s nervous, she and the entire cast are excited to witness the audience’s initial reaction. The eerie, edge of your seat thriller makes its cross-Canada premiere on Crave on Oct. 23. CTV News and Crave are divisions of Bell Media, which is part of BCE Inc.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6m2.text: Image source, Reuters Image caption, Stephen Hubbard pictured in a Moscow courtroom as he was sentenced in 2024 By Maia Davies Published 21 October 2026, 10:22 BST Updated 11 minutes ago Russia has agreed to release a 74-year-old American citizen who was jailed for allegedly fighting on behalf of Ukraine. Stephen Hubbard has been taken to Pulkovo Airport, Putin said during talks with US envoy Steve Witkoff in St Petersburg, according to state media. President Trump said Hubbard was "on his way back home" and "there was no 'swap' necessary for this release". Hubbard, a former teacher originally from Michigan, was sentenced to almost seven years in a penal colony in 2024. Prosecutors had accused him of serving in a defence unit in the eastern city of Izyum when he was captured by Russian forces, shortly after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine two years earlier. Writing on social media after Russian state media reported the release, Trump said it had followed a request he "made directly" to Putin last week. "There was no "swap" necessary for this release," Trump said. The US State Department had previously classified Hubbard as "wrongfully detained" and Trump had suggested on Tuesday that his release may be imminent. "Watch what happens," Trump told reporters, "we have been focused â on âHubbard". CBS News, the BBC's US media partner, reported that Hubbard had been in poor health and was expected to be flown to Texas for treatment. Image source, Rossiya 1 Image caption, President Putin and Witkoff met at the Constantine Palace on Wednesday morning Russian state media reported that Witkoff had thanked Putin for Hubbard's release and, on Trump's behalf, for the deal struck with Washington earlier this month to import Russian diesel . The first shipment under the agreement will leave Russia "in two to three days", Putin said during the meeting, as quoted by state news agency TASS. The diesel deal infuriated Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky and triggered a tumultuous few weeks of deteriorating relations, during which Trump suspended several Russian sanctions and said it was time for Ukraine to elect a new leader. Kyiv meanwhile accused Washington of halting intelligence sharing on deadly Russian strikes , causing Ukrainians to lose their lives - an allegation Washington rejected as "scandalous". The Ukrainian president said on Tuesday that such information sharing had resumed, following talks with Witkoff in Oslo described by the US as "positive". During Wednesday's meeting in St Petersburg, Witkoff was filmed by Russian TV saying the diesel deal was an example to Ukraine of what could be achieved by working together. "Your decision to remove export controls on diesel oil from Russia, not just to the US but also to the world at large in the midst of an economic shock, I think that was really important that that happened," he told Putin. "I know [President Trump] is deeply grateful for it." https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm4g.text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Attacks against Christians have been increasing recently, according to the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church By Ondiro Oganga Published 1 hour ago More than 60 people have been killed in a series of attacks on Christians in Ethiopia's Oromia region, according to the country's Orthodox Church. One resident, whose 75-year-old father was killed, described it as an ambush. "We were completely unprepared and had no prior knowledge. They surrounded us from all four directions," he told BBC Amharic. The regional government said that it would take action against those responsible. A local official blamed the attacks on a newly formed rebel coalition, the Alliance for Survival, which includes the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA). The OLA has not commented but has denied carrying out previous such attacks. A statement from the Holy Synod of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church said that 20 houses were burnt to the ground in the attacks. It did not say who was responsible. Eyewitness told BBC Amharic that five of those killed were children. A church official described the attacks on three areas in the Shirka district as a "massacre", saying security forces arrived at the scene but were unable to stop the assault. Many residents have now fled the area. Condemning the violence, the Orthodox Church said attacks against Christians had been increasing recently, and that "such actions undermine the country's values of mutual respect and peaceful coexistence". In a statement posted on Facebook, the Orthodox Church said it had repeatedly raised concerns about insecurity with authorities at different levels of government, but that "so far there has been no solution". The Ethiopian Human Rights Council, a non-governmental organisation, said in a report released in July 2026 that 458 people had been killed in attacks in that area over the previous four years. But this is one of the most deadly attacks in that period. The report said armed groups had repeatedly targeted local communities, particularly followers of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, in what it described as religiously motivated attacks. The government has previously blamed the OLA for the attacks, with Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed saying violence targeting civilians and religious institutions was part of a plan to destabilise the country. The group, which says it is fighting for greater rights for the Oromo people, denies these allegations. Previous reports have also documented attacks against Muslims in the area. Residents who spoke to the BBC on various occasions have described the violence as both ethnic and religious in nature. About two-thirds of Ethiopians are Christians, mostly Orthodox, while one third are Muslim. https://www.politico.eu/article/whos-who.text: Senior officials from the EU, NATO and key European capitals travel to Abu Dhabi this week to participate in U.S.-brokered talks geared toward ending Russia’s war on Ukraine — allaying fears that Europe risks being completely cut out of the process. The talks coincide with growing concerns in Europe about potential concessions to Russia after Jared Kushner, son-in law and adviser to U.S. President Donald Trump, said last week that discussions would focus on a “new European security architecture” — a phrase often used by Russian officials to mean reducing NATO’s presence in front-line nations and limits on Ukraine’s armed forces. Ukraine will be represented by Rustem Umerov, the head of Kyiv’s foreign intelligence service, along with senior officials Kyrylo Budanov and David Arakhamia. Russia’s contingent is to be led by presidential aide Vladimir Medinsky. Representing the U.S. side will be Kushner and U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff. Advertisement Advertisement The European contingent includes national security advisers from France, the U.K., Germany and Italy, in addition to senior officials from NATO as well as the European Commission and the European Council. The inclusion of EU figures as well as an Italian representative follows a push by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, who warned of fragmentation in a letter to European Council President António Costa last week. Despite their presence in Abu Dhabi, though, the European team is not expected to be inside the room during the main negotiations, according to two senior officials aware of the format. A German official told POLITICO that the format of talks would be “determined as the discussions progress.” The Kremlin has voiced opposition to Europeans directly participating in the talks, according to the same senior officials. Here’s a quick look at the key players from Europe in Abu Dhabi. Günter Sautter (Germany) Sautter is German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s foreign and security policy adviser and a senior career diplomat who has become a major figure in Europe’s efforts to end Russia’s war — and secure a European seat at the negotiating table. Besides representing Germany in the E3 format, Sautter is also coordinating the German-led “Berlin Format” — a German-led coalition to bring together Ukraine, the E3 and other European nations such as Italy, Poland or the Scandinavian countries as well as NATO, EU and others including Canada — that seeks to steer Ukraine’s peace talks and coordinate support for Kyiv. At a press conference with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy last week, Merz remarked that Sautter “is now devoting a significant portion of his workforce to diplomatic efforts to end this war.” Advertisement Advertisement Sautter’s main credo in the talks is that there can be no discussion about a future European security architecture before Russia agrees to a ceasefire. Fabrizio Saggio (Italy) Fabrizio Saggio, diplomatic adviser to Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, will also attend the talks, according to an Italian official. Saggio, whose surname means “wise” in Italian, has earned the not-particularly-original sobriquet “Mister Wolf” in the Italian press, a reference to his role as Meloni’s go-to troubleshooter on major international issues, resolving problems and providing strategic advice. Rustem Umerov attends a press conference in Istanbul, Turkey on July 23, 2025. | Yasin Akgul/AFP via Getty Images Meloni met him during a visit to Tunis, where he was serving as Italian ambassador, to sign a migration deal. “It took her 20 minutes to realize that he was the one” for the job, an Italian diplomat said. In a letter sent to European Council President António Costa last week and seen by POLITICO , Meloni complained about the proliferation of negotiating formats on Ukraine. She called for this week’s informal gathering of EU leaders in Dublin to also discuss Ukraine and decide “once and for all, who sits at the negotiating table representing the European Union, and with what mandate.” Costa agreed to put the issue on the agenda. In the same letter, Meloni also said: “I am not asking for a seat for Italy in this or that format.” But she got one anyway. Advertisement Advertisement Geoffrey van Leeuwen (NATO) Geoffrey van Leeuwen is NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte’s chief of staff. A career diplomat who has served everywhere from Kabul to Mumbai, van Leeuwen is a longtime Rutte loyalist who was trade minister and national security adviser during the boss’ time as Dutch prime minister. Known as an affable and sharp operator who largely shuns the public eye, van Leeuwen helped steer NATO through seemingly unending crises mostly prompted by Donald Trump this year, including the U.S. President’s push to annex Greenland and the fallout from the U.S. war in Iran. NATO doesn’t formally have any role in negotiating a peace deal. But where the talks touch on alliance issues — troop movements, security guarantees or Ukraine’s NATO accession — van Leeuwen will have an interest. His task is primarily “to observe, report back” and make sure “NATO is aware of what’s being said,” said an official familiar with the matter. Jonathan Powell (United Kingdom) U.K. National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell is expected to attend on behalf of the U.K. The former aide to Tony Blair, known for his role in the Northern Ireland peace process, was brought back into government under Keir Starmer and stayed on under Andy Burnham. He has since become one of London’s most reliable links to Washington and is known to have a particularly strong relationship with Witkoff. His position has come under scrutiny in recent months, however, with reports that he is on his way out of Downing Street. Advertisement Advertisement Bjoern Seibert (European Commission) Ursula von der Leyen’s chief of Cabinet is her most trusted lieutenant and one of the most influential figures in Brussels. A close confidant who helps steer her political and diplomatic work, Seibert is a central player in the EU’s discussions on Ukraine. His presence in Abu Dhabi puts von der Leyen’s office in the mix as Kyiv, Washington and Moscow discuss the war. He has joined earlier rounds of Ukraine talks, including meetings in Miami and Oslo with U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff, where officials discussed security guarantees, territory and Ukraine’s postwar recovery. Jonathan Powell leaves No. 10 Downing St. in London on Oct. 24, 2025. | Leon Neal/Getty Images Seibert will play a similar role to the national security advisers of the E3 countries and NATO’s van Leeuwen, and will be present at whatever tables they’re sitting at, according to an EU official. But the Europeans are likely to be briefed separately because the Kremlin has repeatedly objected to them being present in the room for the three-way talks, including on Monday . Anna-Maria Boura (European Council) As European Council President António Costa’s chief foreign policy adviser, Boura will be the EU’s member countries’ eyes in Abu Dhabi. Her place on the ground marks the Council’s return to the Ukraine talks, after Costa’s office was absent from earlier rounds in Miami and Oslo , where Seibert represented the Commission. Advertisement Advertisement Boura’s profile is rising as Pedro Lourtie, Costa’s chief of Cabinet, is expected to leave for a new diplomatic role in the U.S . (It was Lourtie who opened a channel to the Kremlin this summer , speaking by phone with an official close to Vladimir Putin.) Boura also played a key part in the EU-Canada summit, holding the pen on the bloc’s side of the work on the joint declaration. Emmanuel Bonne (France) As Emmanuel Macron’s chief diplomatic adviser, Emmanuel Bonne is the man called upon to jet off to key venues — like Abu Dhabi this week — to lay the groundwork for the French president’s most important geopolitical initiatives. Bonne, a career diplomat who served in multiple postings in the Middle East, joined Macron’s team in 2019 — a long tenure at the Elysée compared to some of his peers. Bonne was reportedly headed toward the exit in January 2025 due to a major dispute with the president’s chief of military staff, but Macron convinced him to stay on.
